title: Browser extension toolkit (install once, used across phases)

plan.summary: A browser extension toolkit adds framework, performance, accessibility, SEO and security views that built-in DevTools does not give.

prerequisites.bridge: Built-in browser panels that inspect and debug a live page.
A small add-on program that adds features to the browser.
The DOM is the tree of objects the browser builds from HTML.
The browser sends a request; the server returns status, headers and body.

outcomes: Explain how a framework devtools extension reads component state from a page.
Explain what automated accessibility and SEO checks catch and what they miss.
Build a script that audits extension manifests for risky permissions.
Build an accessibility and SEO check that runs on every release page.
Decide when to use an extension instead of a built-in DevTools panel.

lesson_outline.title: Why an extension toolkit: what built-in DevTools does not show
lesson_outline.visual_reason: An extension runs in separate parts (content script, service worker, DevTools page) with permissions; a diagram shows which part can see the page and which can see the network.
lesson_outline.interaction_goal: Sort extension capabilities into the part that owns them and the permission they need.

lesson_outline.title: Framework devtools: see components, state and renders
lesson_outline.visual_reason: A framework devtools extension reads the component tree and records commits; the learner changes state and watches the tree, props and Profiler commits change.
lesson_outline.interaction_goal: Change a prop or dispatch an action and predict which components re-render and what the store holds after time travel.

lesson_outline.title: Performance extensions: wasted renders and field data
lesson_outline.visual_reason: Lab data from one load and field data from real users give different numbers; a side-by-side view shows why both are needed.
lesson_outline.interaction_goal: Match each performance question to the tool that answers it: React Scan, Web Vitals overlay, Lighthouse or a CrUX viewer.

lesson_outline.title: Accessibility extensions: automated checks and their limits
lesson_outline.visual_reason: Contrast ratio and rule results change with color and markup; the learner adjusts colors and structure and watches which checks pass and which still need a human.
lesson_outline.interaction_goal: Change text and background colors and heading levels, and predict which axe or WAVE rules fail.

lesson_outline.title: SEO extensions: rendered source, redirects and structured data
lesson_outline.visual_reason: A crawler sees the source HTML, the rendered DOM and the redirect chain at different times; a diagram shows where each SEO extension reads.
lesson_outline.interaction_goal: Name which extension reveals a missing title that exists only after JavaScript runs.

lesson_outline.title: Security and privacy extensions: libraries, headers and cookies
lesson_outline.visual_reason: A security check is a sequence of decisions (fingerprint, check libraries, read headers, test with a blocker); a branching deck lets the learner pick the next check for a symptom.
lesson_outline.interaction_goal: Choose the right extension for each security symptom and order a quick security pass.

lesson_outline.title: Design, API helpers and a team extension profile in practice
lesson_outline.visual_reason: A team profile groups vetted extensions by phase and permission level; a diagram shows the profile and where design and API helpers fit.
lesson_outline.interaction_goal: Sort candidate extensions into keep, replace with a built-in panel, or reject for permissions.

mini_projects.use_case: A team lead must approve extensions for the company browser profile; a Node.js script reads each extension manifest and flags broad host permissions and risky APIs.
A content site checks every release page; a script runs axe-core and reads title, meta and structured data, and fails CI on new problems.

capstone.name: toolkit-profile CLI
capstone.problem: A frontend team keeps one vetted browser extension profile; a Node.js CLI validates the list against a permission policy, prints a setup checklist, and runs accessibility, SEO and security-header checks on a URL.

goals: master frontend engineering end to end from the N1 roadmap
learn visually and by experimenting with simulations
install one extension toolkit used across later phases

curriculum.scope: Browser extensions a frontend developer installs once and uses across the roadmap: framework devtools, performance, accessibility, SEO, security and privacy, design and CSS, and API and data helpers, plus how extensions work and how to vet them.
